report.source_text: A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was performed at the referring hospital, and it showed a segment of circumferential wall thickening affecting the proximal descending colon, 6.3 cm long, with a maximum wall thickness of 1.6 cm. Peri-colonic fat stranding and multifocal regional nodules and lymph nodes were identified. Multiple peritoneal deposits were seen, and the largest deposit was seen along the mesenteric margin, measuring 4.9×3 cm. There was no definitive involvement of adjacent structures. There were innumerable hypovascular ring-enhancing hepatic masses scattered in both lobes involving all liver segments, and the largest was located at segment 4b, measuring 8.1 cm. There was also necrotic lymphadenopathy seen at the gastrohepatic ligament. The lungs were clear, with no suspicious pulmonary nodules

report.source_text: Histopathological examination of the descending colon biopsy demonstrated dual morphologies in which a predominant component comprised of tumor cells arranged in nested, organoid, and rosette-like growth patterns with a focal area of solid sheet associated with brisk mitotic activity estimated at 30 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields (Figure 3A). The second minor component (30%) exhibited intermingled malignant glandular structures morphologically consistent with adenocarcinoma (Figure 3B). The predominant component was diffusely positive for Pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3) and Synaptophysin and negative for Chromogranin immunohisto-chemical stains, whereas adenocarcinoma was negative for the neuroendocrine markers (Figure 3C, 3D).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 48-year-old man with diabetes mellitus and ulcerative colitis presented with 1-month history of right upper-quadrant pain, fatigue, constipation for 6 days, and significant weight loss of approximately 18 kg. Physical examination revealed a palpable epigastric mass; vital signs were stable, afebrile, with no jaundice or pallor. Laboratory investigations and tumor markers were normal. CT imaging of chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 6.3 cm circumferential wall-thickening lesion in the proximal descending colon with 1.6 cm maximum wall thickness, peri-colonic fat stranding, and regional nodules. Extensive metastatic disease was identified: innumerable hypovascular ring-enhancing hepatic masses scattered in both lobes (largest 8.1 cm at segment 4b), multiple peritoneal deposits (largest 4.9×3 cm along mesenteric margin), and necrotic lymphadenopathy at the gastrohepatic ligament. Colonoscopy confirmed circumferential wall thickening, from which biopsy was obtained and stenting was performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated dual morphologies: a predominant neuroendocrine component (70%) with nested, organoid, and rosette-like growth patterns with focal solid sheets and brisk mitotic activity (30 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields), and a minor adenocarcinoma component (30%). Immunohistochemistry showed the neuroendocrine component was diffusely positive for Pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3) and Synaptophysin, and negative for Chromogranin, while the adenocarcinoma component was negative for neuroendocrine markers. The patient was diagnosed with metastatic poorly differentiated MANEC of the colon, deemed unresectable. He was referred to medical oncology and received 9 cycles of cisplatin and etoposide chemotherapy, which showed good response with regression of the primary tumor, liver, and bony metastases. He subsequently developed right retinal vein thrombosis.
